questions.q: If a rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm, can you determine its exact area? Answer yes or no and give a reason.
questions.a: No, because multiple rectangles with perimeter 20 cm exist (e.g., 6×4 gives area 24 cm², 7×3 gives 21 cm², 9×1 gives 9 cm²). A wrong answer of "yes" reveals the student thinks perimeter uniquely fixes the dimensions, confusing the formula P = 2(l+w) with a single solution for l and w.

questions.q: Two different shapes have the same perimeter. Student A says they must have the same area because the boundary length is identical. Student B says the areas can be different. Who is correct and why?
questions.a: Student B is correct. Perimeter is a one-dimensional measure of the boundary, while area is a two-dimensional measure of the interior. The same length of boundary can enclose different amounts of space depending on the shape's configuration. A wrong answer choosing Student A shows the student conflates linear and square measures, not recognizing that area depends on how the boundary is arranged.

questions.q: A wire of length 36 cm is bent into a square. The same wire is then bent into a rectangle with length 13 cm. Find the area of each shape and state which shape encloses more area.
questions.a: Square: side = 36/4 = 9 cm, area = 9×9 = 81 cm². Rectangle: perimeter = 36 = 2(13 + breadth) → breadth = 5 cm, area = 13×5 = 65 cm². The square encloses more area (81 cm² > 65 cm²). A wrong answer might miscalculate breadth as 36 - 13 = 23 cm, showing confusion between perimeter and semi-perimeter, or forget to divide by 2.

questions.q: Consider all rectangles with a fixed perimeter of 24 cm. As the length increases from 1 cm to 11 cm, how does the area change? Describe the pattern and explain why it happens.
questions.a: Area increases from 11 cm² (1×11) to a maximum of 36 cm² (6×6 square), then decreases symmetrically to 11 cm² (11×1). This happens because area = l × (12 - l) = 12l - l², a quadratic that peaks when l = 6. A wrong answer stating area always increases or always decreases reveals the student hasn't explored the full range or doesn't see the symmetric relationship between length and breadth.

questions.q: A student claims: "If you increase the perimeter of a shape, its area will always increase." Evaluate this statement with a counterexample or proof.
questions.a: The statement is false. Counterexample: A 10×1 rectangle has perimeter 22 cm and area 10 cm². A 6×6 square has perimeter 24 cm (larger) and area 36 cm² (larger). But a 20×1 rectangle has perimeter 42 cm (larger than 24) and area 20 cm² (smaller than 36). So increasing perimeter does not guarantee increased area. A wrong answer agreeing with the claim shows the student assumes a direct proportional relationship between perimeter and area.

questions.q: Design two different shapes (not rectangles) that have the same perimeter but very different areas. Draw them on grid paper, label dimensions, and calculate both perimeters and areas to verify.
questions.a: Example: A right triangle with legs 6 cm and 8 cm (hypotenuse 10 cm) has perimeter 24 cm and area 24 cm². A regular hexagon with side 4 cm has perimeter 24 cm and area ≈ 41.6 cm². Both have perimeter 24 cm but different areas. A poor answer might use two rectangles, which doesn't show the concept extends beyond rectangles, or might not verify calculations, indicating lack of precision.
